newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU assembly plans stinging attack on new EU treaty.
newsitem.headline: EU assembly plans stinging attack on new EU treaty.

text.p: The European Parliament is expected to launch a blistering attack on June 11 on the draft of a new European Union treaty, prepared by the Dutch, which EU leaders are due to sign in Amsterdam six days later.

The new treaty falls far short of the far-reaching reforms EU leaders pledged to make in March 1996 when they began talks on changes designed to prepare the 15-member EU bloc for an ambitious eastward expansion early next century, the parliament is due to say in a highly critical resolution.

The text drawn up by the Dutch, who hold the EU presidency until the end of June, is inadequate on a wide variety of counts and could even set the development of the EU back, according to a draft of the resolution obtained by Reuters.

The planned reforms will not make the EU's major institutions sufficiently more efficient or democratic, or better able to cope with a Union which could eventually have 25 members, the EU assembly's resolution says.

Nor does the new treaty provide the EU, which is hell bent on monetary union, with sufficient power to take joint action on other issues closer to its citizens' heart, such as foreign policy, jobs and social concerns, the criticism adds.

Catherine Lalumiere, the French leader of the left-wing Radical party in the European Parliament, went even further on Thursday, calling for the whole EU reform process to be delayed to give the new French and British Socialist governments time to try to improve on a draft treaty negotiated by their right-wing predecessors.
"It's only good sense," Lalumiere told Reuters. "If the text on the table had got widespread approval it would be different but the text has provoked a lot of criticism."

"Let's seize the opportunity to extend negotiations -- not too long because we don't want to delay the introduction of the single currency or enlargement to the east, but enough to try and push reforms further," Lalumiere said.

She suggested a delay until September might give the governments of Lionel Jospin in Paris and Tony Blair in London time to push for better deals than those worked out by former French and British prime minsters Alain Juppe and John Major.
She said she had not put her proposal to either government, or to the Dutch, for whom the Amsterdam summit is the crowning point of their six months at the EU helm.

Political analysts said on Monday that the shift to the centre-left in Europe, where only Germany and Spain continue to have purely conservative administrations, could spur the EU to deeper integration on social issues but was unlikey to have a major impact on the Amsterdam summit.
"Everybody wants this over," said one EU diplomat.
